history.heading: Swedish roots
paragraphs: The Åland Islands, an archipelago of more than 6,500 islands and skerries at the entrance to the Gulf of Bothnia, have been inhabited since the Stone Age. In the Viking Age and the Middle Ages they were closely tied to Sweden, and Swedish became the language of the islanders.

For centuries Åland was part of the Swedish kingdom, which then included Finland. Its strategic position between Stockholm and the Finnish coast made it important for shipping and naval power in the Baltic Sea.

history.heading: Russian rule and demilitarisation
paragraphs: In 1809 Sweden ceded Finland, together with Åland, to the Russian Empire. The Russians built the large fortress of Bomarsund, which was destroyed by British and French forces during the Crimean War in 1854. The peace treaty of 1856 declared Åland demilitarised, a status that continues today.

When Finland became independent in 1917, many Ålanders wished to rejoin Sweden. The dispute was referred to the League of Nations, which in 1921 decided that Åland would belong to Finland but with extensive self-government and guarantees for its Swedish language and culture.

history.heading: Autonomy
paragraphs: Åland's first autonomy act came into force in 1922, and the islands have had their own parliament since then. The autonomy arrangement is often cited internationally as a successful example of resolving a minority dispute peacefully.
When Finland joined the European Union in 1995, Åland joined too, but with special arrangements, including being outside the EU tax area.

culture.heading: Language and identity
paragraphs: Swedish is the only official language of Åland, and almost all residents speak it as their first language. Ålanders have a strong regional identity, with their own flag, postage stamps and internet domain (.ax).
Ålanders hold a special regional citizenship, which is required to vote in local elections and to buy land freely on the islands.

culture.heading: Maritime heritage and traditions
paragraphs: Seafaring has shaped Ålandic life for centuries. Mariehamn, the capital, was home to one of the last fleets of large sailing ships in the world in the early 20th century, and the four-masted barque Pommern is preserved there as a museum ship.

Midsummer is the year's most important celebration, marked by tall decorated midsummer poles. Local food traditions include Åland pancake, a baked semolina or rice pudding dish served with prune compote and whipped cream.

politics.heading: Self-government
paragraphs: Åland is an autonomous region of Finland. Its parliament, the Lagting, makes laws on matters such as education, culture, health, policing and the local economy, while Finland retains responsibility for foreign affairs, most taxation and the courts.
The government of Åland, the Landskapsregering, is headed by a premier (lantråd). Åland elects one member to the Finnish parliament.

politics.heading: Demilitarised and neutral
paragraphs: Under international agreements, Åland is demilitarised and neutralised: no military forces may be stationed there and residents with Ålandic citizenship are exempt from Finnish military service. Finland's accession to NATO in 2023 did not change this status.

economy.heading: Shipping and services
paragraphs: Shipping is the backbone of Åland's economy. The islands lie on the busy ferry routes between Finland and Sweden, and because Åland is outside the EU tax area, ferries that stop there can sell tax-free goods, which has long supported passenger traffic.
Tourism, banking, insurance and public services are also important, and Åland enjoys a relatively high standard of living. The currency is the euro.

economy.heading: Agriculture and fishing
paragraphs: Agriculture benefits from the mild maritime climate. Apples, potatoes, onions and dairy products are notable, and food processing, such as potato chips, is a local industry. Fishing and fish farming also contribute.
